course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: An Age of Reform
lesson.summary: How religious revival, voluntary organizations, abolitionism, and the women's rights movement tried to improve American society between 1800 and 1848.
learningGoals: Explain how and why reform movements such as temperance and education reform developed.
Explain how abolitionism and antislavery movements grew in the North and what limits they faced.
Explain how the women's rights movement expressed its ideals at Seneca Falls.
lesson.bigIdea: Inspired by the Second Great Awakening and by democratic ideals, Americans formed voluntary organizations outside of government to improve society, and those efforts included antislavery and women's rights movements.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain how and why various reform movements developed and expanded. For each movement, name the problem it identified, who led it, how it worked outside government, and how much it achieved.

sections.title: Voluntary organizations and reform

blocks.text: Americans formed new voluntary organizations that aimed to change individual behaviors and improve society through temperance and other reform efforts. The American Temperance Society (1826) urged Americans to give up alcohol, which reformers blamed for poverty, violence, and family suffering. Horace Mann in Massachusetts promoted public schools, and Dorothea Dix pressed states to build asylums to care for the mentally ill and to improve prisons.

The Second Great Awakening also inspired utopian communities, which tried to create model societies. Some, such as the Shakers, were religious, and others, such as New Harmony in Indiana and Brook Farm in Massachusetts, were based on cooperative ideals.

sections.takeaway: Voluntary groups worked outside government to reduce drinking, expand schools, reform asylums and prisons, and build model communities.

sections.title: Abolitionism and antislavery movements

blocks.text: Abolitionist and antislavery movements gradually achieved emancipation in the North, contributing to the growth of the free African American population, even as many state governments restricted African Americans' rights. By the 1820s most Northern states had abolished slavery or put it on the path to ending. Early antislavery efforts included the American Colonization Society (1816), which proposed sending free Black Americans to Africa, and most African Americans rejected this plan.

In the 1830s a more radical abolitionist movement called for immediate emancipation. William Lloyd Garrison began publishing The Liberator in 1831, and the American Anti-Slavery Society formed in 1833. Frederick Douglass, a formerly enslaved man, became one of the movement's greatest speakers. Antislavery movements increased in the North, but they faced hostility. Mobs attacked abolitionists, Congress adopted a rule in 1836 to table antislavery petitions without discussion, and many Northerners opposed equal rights for African Americans.

sections.takeaway: Abolitionists moved from gradual emancipation toward demands for immediate freedom, in the face of strong opposition.

sections.title: The women's rights movement

blocks.text: A women's rights movement sought to create greater equality and opportunities for women, expressing its ideals at the Seneca Falls Convention. Many of its leaders began in the temperance and antislavery movements, where women learned to organize but often found themselves restricted. In 1848 Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized the convention at Seneca Falls, New York. It adopted the Declaration of Sentiments, which was modeled on the Declaration of Independence and listed the ways in which women were denied rights, including the right to vote, to own property, and to receive an equal education.

Over time, arguments emerged over whether to narrow the goals to white women. Black women such as Sojourner Truth took part in the movement, but disagreements about race divided the movement in later decades.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Seneca Falls did not win the vote for women. It was the beginning of a long campaign that continued until the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.

sections.takeaway: At Seneca Falls, reformers adapted the language of the Declaration of Independence to demand equal rights for women.

connections.title: Antislavery voices and African American communities
connections.body: African Americans were central to the antislavery movement and created their own organizations. Topic 4.12 follows their experience.
connections.transferQuestion: Why did many reformers who worked in the temperance and antislavery movements turn to women's rights?
connections.feedback: A strong answer notes that women gained organizing experience in those movements but were often kept from speaking and voting, and that this led them to question their own rights.
